title: Tablet IX
paragraphs: Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his comrade Enkidu as he roamed the open country: “Shall I not die too, just like Enkidu? Sorrow has come into my heart. I am afraid of death as I roam the open country. I will set out on the road to Utnapishtim, the son of Ubara-Tutu, and I will travel fast.

“If I reach the gates of the mountains in darkness and meet lions there, and terror falls on me, I will lift my head to the sky and pray to the Moon-god. Let my prayer reach the gods: ‘Save me!’ ” He slept, and saw a dream, and saw creatures rejoicing in life. He raised his axe in his hand, drew his sword from his belt, and leapt among them like a spear, striking and crushing.

The name of the hills was Mashu. He reached the mountains of Mashu, which keep watch every day over the rising and setting of the Sun-god. Their peaks reach up to the height of heaven, and their flanks reach down deep into the underworld. At their gates stand Scorpion-men on guard, terrible and frightening, whose very glance is death. Their splendour is overwhelming and shakes the hills. They are the wardens of Shamash at his rising and his setting. As soon as Gilgamesh saw them his face went pale with fear and dread, and he threw himself down in front of them, out of his senses.

Then the Scorpion-man said to his wife: “Look, the one coming toward us has a body made of the flesh of the gods.” His wife answered the Scorpion-man: “Two parts of him are god, and only a third of him is human.”

The Scorpion-man spoke to Gilgamesh, asked him why he had come on so far a journey, and told him how hard the crossing was. Gilgamesh told him that he meant to ask Utnapishtim about death and life. But the Scorpion-man said that no one had ever made that journey, that no one had ever crossed the mountains. The way through was the Road of the Sun, a journey of twenty-four hours that began in deep darkness. He described the journey to him hour by hour, and Gilgamesh accepted the test of his strength: “Even if it is in pain, even if my face is weathered by cold and heat, even if I go in grief, I will go.” Then the Scorpion-man, with a last word about the mountains of Mashu, said goodbye and wished him success. When Gilgamesh heard this, he set off at the Scorpion-man’s word and took the Road of the Sun. For the first two hours there was deep darkness and no light, and it did not let him see what lay behind him. Each two hours after that was the same until he had passed the eighth; at the ninth he came to the first glimmer of light. At last, at the twelfth double hour, he came out into the full blaze of the sun, and there he saw the Tree of the Gods.
Its fruit was all of red stone, and it was hung about with tendrils. It was lovely to look at. Its foliage was of lapis blue, and it bore fruit that delighted the eye.

“He has dressed himself in the skins of wild animals and eats their flesh. Gilgamesh, there will never be a crossing where there has never been one, not for as long as the wind drives the water.” Shamash was moved, and he called to Gilgamesh and spoke to him:

“Gilgamesh, why are you running, when you will not find the life you are looking for?” Gilgamesh answered the warrior Shamash: “After I have roamed up and down the wilderness as a wanderer, am I to lay my head in the depths of the earth and sleep there through all the years, for ever and ever? Let my eyes see the sun and be filled with its brightness. The darkness is driven far away when the brightness is wide. When will a dead man ever look on the light of the sun?”
